objective: Provide an expert-level, implementation-oriented outline of modern C++ covering language fundamentals, object lifetime, RAII, value categories, templates, concepts, generic programming, STL, memory management, concurrency, coroutines, modules, metaprogramming, compile-time programming, exceptions, ABI and linkage, performance, tooling, testing, interoperability, and production architecture.
scope: Modern ISO C++ with emphasis on C++20 and C++23 concepts and facilities, while maintaining the historical context necessary to understand C++11 through C++23 evolution. Focus on portable language and standard-library semantics rather than compiler-specific extensions.

sections.name: C++ Foundations
sections.purpose: Establish syntax, translation units, declarations, definitions, expressions, statements, namespaces, scopes, and the compilation model.

sections.name: Type System
sections.purpose: Explain C++'s static type system, object representations, conversions, qualifiers, compound types, and type traits.

subsections.name: References and Pointers

sections.name: Classes, Objects, and Encapsulation
sections.purpose: Model C++ object-oriented facilities, class invariants, access control, constructors, destructors, methods, and object representation.

subsections.name: Encapsulation
examples: class Account { private: int balance_; public: int balance() const; };

sections.name: Object Lifetime, RAII, and Resource Management
sections.purpose: Explain one of C++'s central design models: deterministic object lifetime combined with ownership-aware resource management.

subsections.name: Storage Duration
examples: Local objects normally have automatic storage duration.

sections.name: Value Categories, Moves, and Copy Semantics
sections.purpose: Explain lvalues, prvalues, xvalues, move construction, move assignment, copy semantics, and temporary materialization.

subsections.name: Rule of Zero and Special Member Functions
examples: Prefer member types whose destructors and ownership semantics make custom special members unnecessary.

sections.name: Inheritance and Polymorphism
sections.purpose: Cover class inheritance, virtual dispatch, abstract interfaces, multiple inheritance, and object-oriented substitution.

subsections.name: Virtual Dispatch
details: vtable implementation as common ABI technique
examples: struct Shape { virtual double area() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default; };

sections.name: Templates and Generic Programming
sections.purpose: Explain compile-time polymorphism, template declaration, deduction, specialization, instantiation, and generic design.

subsections.name: Template Fundamentals
examples: template<class T> T max_value(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }

sections.name: Concepts and Constraints
sections.purpose: Explain modern C++ constraints as a structured alternative to many historical SFINAE techniques.

subsections.name: Concept Definitions
examples: template<class T> concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; };

subsections.name: Constrained Interfaces
examples: template<Addable T> T add(T a, T b) { return a + b; }

sections.name: Standard Library and STL
sections.purpose: Provide a systematic model of standard containers, iterators, algorithms, ranges, utilities, strings, numerics, and resource abstractions.

sections.name: Exceptions and Error Handling
sections.purpose: Cover C++ exception semantics, exception safety, error-value approaches, and modern alternatives.

subsections.name: Exceptions
examples: try { operation(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { handle(e); }

subsections.name: Exception Safety
examples: Design operations so resource invariants remain valid when an exception is thrown.

sections.name: Memory Safety and Undefined Behavior
sections.purpose: Identify the major classes of memory and language-level undefined behavior that must be controlled in C++.

subsections.name: Lifetime Hazards
examples: Do not retain a reference to an object after its lifetime ends.

subsections.name: Pointer and Bounds Hazards
examples: Prefer standard containers and ownership abstractions to reduce manual pointer management.

sections.name: Concurrency and Parallelism
sections.purpose: Explain C++ threading, synchronization, atomics, futures, tasks, memory ordering, and parallel algorithms.

sections.name: Coroutines
sections.purpose: Explain the C++ coroutine machinery introduced in C++20 and the abstractions built on top of it.

subsections.name: Coroutine Abstractions
examples: A library can build task or generator abstractions around the standard coroutine machinery.

sections.name: Compile-Time Programming and Metaprogramming
sections.purpose: Cover constexpr, consteval, constinit, type traits, compile-time evaluation, and template metaprogramming.

subsections.name: Constant Evaluation
examples: constexpr int square(int x) { return x * x; }

subsections.name: Type-Level Computation
examples: template<class... Ts> constexpr std::size_t count = sizeof...(Ts);

sections.name: Modules and Modern Translation Architecture
sections.purpose: Explain C++ modules as a modern alternative and complement to traditional header inclusion.

sections.name: Linkage, ABI, and Binary Compatibility
sections.purpose: Explain how C++ source code becomes linkable binaries and why ABI boundaries are difficult to maintain.

subsections.name: One Definition Rule
examples: Identical definitions may be required across translation units depending on entity category.

subsections.name: ABI Boundaries
examples: extern "C" can suppress C++ name mangling for compatible interfaces.

sections.name: Performance Engineering
sections.purpose: Explain C++ performance characteristics through measurement, data representation, allocation, locality, optimization, and concurrency.

subsections.name: Data-Oriented Performance
examples: Prefer contiguous storage when access patterns benefit from locality.

subsections.name: Compiler Optimization
examples: Measure release builds rather than extrapolating from debug performance.

sections.name: Build Systems and Tooling
sections.purpose: Cover compilation, dependency management, build configuration, static analysis, formatting, debugging, sanitization, and CI.

subsections.name: Compilation Pipeline
examples: source -> preprocessing -> compilation -> object -> linking -> executable

subsections.name: Debugging
examples: Use a debugger together with sanitizer output for memory and lifetime failures.

sections.name: Testing and Verification
sections.purpose: Cover unit, integration, property, fuzz, compile-time, concurrency, and performance testing.

subsections.name: Fuzzing and Property Testing
examples: Fuzz parsers and serialization boundaries with malformed and adversarial inputs.

sections.name: Interoperability and FFI
sections.purpose: Explain integration with C, operating-system APIs, foreign runtimes, and language-neutral binary interfaces.

subsections.name: Platform APIs
examples: Wrap platform handles in RAII types.

sections.name: Production Architecture and Design
sections.purpose: Apply C++ language facilities to maintainable large-scale systems.

subsections.name: Ownership Architecture
examples: Prefer unique ownership unless shared lifetime is an explicit requirement.

subsections.name: pImpl and ABI Stability
examples: class Widget { struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_; };

relationships.relationship: RAII uses deterministic object lifetime to manage resources automatically.
Destructors provide automatic cleanup during normal scope exit and stack unwinding.
Expression categories determine how objects can bind to references and participate in move operations.
Concepts constrain template interfaces and improve overload selection and diagnostics.
The standard library relies extensively on generic programming.
Classic STL algorithms operate over iterator-based ranges.
Ranges use concepts to express iterator and range requirements.
Synchronization and atomic ordering are defined in terms of the C++ memory model.
Coroutines provide suspension and resumption machinery that libraries can use to implement asynchronous systems.
Module dependency discovery and compilation require build-system support.
Interoperability depends on compatible calling conventions, layouts, symbols, and ownership contracts.
Runtime instrumentation can detect many classes of memory, lifetime, threading, and undefined-behavior defects.
Layout, allocation, indirection, and locality directly influence performance characteristics.

dependencies.name: C++ compiler
dependencies.purpose: Parses, type-checks, instantiates, optimizes, and generates code from C++ translation units.

dependencies.name: linker
dependencies.purpose: Combines object files and libraries into executable or shared binary artifacts.

dependencies.name: standard library
dependencies.purpose: Provides containers, algorithms, utilities, concurrency primitives, I/O, memory facilities, and language-support components.

dependencies.name: build system
dependencies.purpose: Coordinates compilation, dependencies, linking, testing, installation, and configuration.

dependencies.name: debugger
dependencies.purpose: Provides runtime inspection, breakpoints, stack traces, and debugging facilities.

dependencies.name: sanitizer instrumentation
dependencies.purpose: Detects selected classes of memory, undefined-behavior, and concurrency errors.

edge_cases.handling: Ensure referenced objects outlive all references and account for temporary and container invalidation rules.
Understand container-specific invalidation rules before retaining iterators or references across mutations.
Use references, pointers, or polymorphic ownership when preserving dynamic type is required.
Use a virtual destructor when deleting derived objects through a base pointer is part of the interface.
Use weak_ptr for non-owning edges where cycles would otherwise prevent destruction.
Use appropriate synchronization or atomic operations; a data race is not merely a logical race and can result in undefined behavior.
Avoid fragile cross-translation-unit initialization dependencies and use controlled initialization patterns.
Ensure entities requiring consistent definitions have compatible definitions across translation units.
Rely on RAII and member destruction while designing constructors to preserve class invariants.
Understand how noexcept affects container relocation and exception guarantees.
Control template complexity, translation-unit boundaries, code generation, and repeated instantiation.
Define explicit binary interface contracts and avoid exposing unstable implementation details across ABI boundaries.
Ensure coroutine frames, promise objects, awaited resources, and referenced state remain valid for the required duration.
Combine testing with compiler diagnostics, sanitizers, static analysis, and careful lifetime reasoning.

constraints: The C++ abstract machine defines program semantics independently of any single hardware implementation.
Undefined behavior must not be treated as a recoverable runtime condition.
Ownership and lifetime contracts should be explicit in interfaces.
RAII should be preferred for resource management.
Manual memory management should be justified by a concrete ownership or performance requirement.
Concurrency must respect the C++ memory model.
Atomic ordering must match the synchronization guarantees required by the algorithm.
ABI-sensitive interfaces must account for compiler, standard-library, platform, layout, and calling-convention compatibility.
Templates and concepts should express generic requirements without unnecessarily increasing compile-time complexity.
Performance claims should be validated through representative measurement.
Compiler-specific extensions should be isolated when portability is a requirement.
Public APIs should minimize accidental exposure of implementation details.
Unsafe operations involving raw memory, casts, lifetime manipulation, and low-level synchronization require explicit invariant reasoning.

validation.check: The program compiles under the intended C++ standard mode and supported compiler set.
All objects, references, pointers, iterators, and resources obey their required lifetime constraints.
Ownership transfer, destruction, copying, and moving are explicit and correct.
Conversions, overloads, templates, concepts, and polymorphic interfaces express the intended type relationships.
The implementation is reviewed and instrumented for major classes of undefined behavior.
Synchronization, atomic ordering, thread lifetime, and shared-state access satisfy the required happens-before relationships.
Operations preserve documented invariants under exceptions and use appropriate exception guarantees.
Binary interfaces are compatible across intended compiler, platform, and library boundaries.
Unit, integration, fuzz, sanitizer, concurrency, and regression tests cover critical behavior.
Performance-sensitive behavior is measured using representative workloads and appropriate profiling tools.
Warnings, static analysis, formatting, sanitizers, builds, tests, and CI checks pass.
Platform assumptions and compiler extensions are identified and isolated where portability matters.

open_questions: Should the next iteration focus on C++23 language and library facilities exclusively, or retain C++11-C++23 historical progression?
Should the object model and lifetime model be expanded into a formal treatment of storage, object lifetime, pointer validity, and aliasing?
Should templates receive a deeper compiler-oriented treatment covering deduction, overload resolution, instantiation, SFINAE, concepts, and constraint normalization?
Should undefined behavior be expanded into a dedicated taxonomy covering lifetime, bounds, aliasing, concurrency, initialization, arithmetic, and library preconditions?
Should concurrency be expanded into a formal C++ memory-model hierarchy covering sequenced-before, synchronizes-with, happens-before, atomics, and memory-order relations?
Should coroutines be expanded into a complete promise/awaiter/awaitable design model?
Should modules include migration strategies from header-heavy legacy systems?
Should the standard library be expanded into a complete namespace-by-namespace reference?
Should build architecture include CMake, Ninja, package managers, cross-compilation, reproducible builds, and CI/CD?
Should production architecture include game engines, embedded systems, high-performance computing, networking, desktop applications, and large-scale backend systems as separate application domains?
